courses.title: Finding Your Way
courses.summary: pwd, ls, cd and paths: move through any filesystem with confidence.
courses.intro: Every terminal session starts *somewhere*. Before you can read, search or change anything, you need to know where you are and how to get where you want to go. This course is a small map of a filesystem with four directions and one hidden gem.

files.README:
Welcome, traveller.

This lab is a tiny map of a filesystem. North, south, east and west are
directories; inside them are files and more directories. Somewhere a gem is
hidden. Walk it with cd, look with ls, and read with cat.
files.east/sunrise.txt: The sun rises in the east. Nothing else to see here, but you got here.
files.north/compass.txt:
The needle points north.

You read this through an ABSOLUTE path: one that starts with / and means
the same thing no matter where you stand.
files.north/forest/owl.txt:
Hoo. You are two levels below the lab now.

Type cd .. to climb one level, or cd - to jump back to where you were.
files.south/.cave/gem.txt:
You found the hidden gem!

Names that start with a dot are hidden from a plain ls. ls -a shows them,
and find walks into them without being asked.
files.south/river.txt:
The river runs south.

If you are reading this from the forest, you used a RELATIVE path: ..
climbs one level, and every / goes one step deeper.
files.west/sunset.txt: The sun sets in the west. Every direction is just a directory.

lessons.title: Where am I?
lessons.body:
A shell always has a **current working directory**: the directory your commands act on unless you name another one.

- `pwd` (*print working directory*) tells you where that is.
- `cd PATH` (*change directory*) moves you there.

A path that starts with `/` is **absolute**. It begins at the very top of the filesystem (the *root*), so it means the same thing wherever you stand.

```
cd /lab/navigator
pwd
```

Real world: the first thing a sysadmin types after logging into an unfamiliar server is often `pwd`. Commands like `rm` act on "here", so knowing where "here" is matters.

objectives.text: Walk into the lab by its absolute path: cd /lab/navigator
objectives.hint: Type exactly: cd /lab/navigator

objectives.text: Ask the shell where you are with pwd
objectives.hint: pwd takes no arguments: just type pwd

lessons.title: Look around
lessons.body:
`ls` lists a directory: the current one by default, or any directory you name (`ls south`).

**Flags** change what a command does. They start with a dash:

- `ls -a` shows **all** entries, including hidden ones. A name that starts with `.` is hidden from a plain `ls`. That's how config files like `.bashrc` stay out of your way.
- `ls -F` adds a marker after each name: `/` for a directory, `*` for an executable.

Flags combine: `ls -aF` is the same as `ls -a -F`.

```
ls
ls -a south
ls -F
```

Real world: `ls -la` is probably the most-typed command on Earth. It's the first look inside any directory, hidden files and all.

objectives.text: List what is in the lab with ls
objectives.hint: From /lab/navigator, type ls

objectives.text: Reveal the hidden entries in south: ls -a south
objectives.hint: The -a flag means all, including names that start with a dot

objectives.text: Tell directories from files with ls -F
objectives.hint: -F adds a / after every directory

lessons.title: Moving around
lessons.body:
A path that does **not** start with `/` is **relative**: it starts from where you are now.

- `cd north/forest` goes into `north`, then into `forest`, in one step.
- `..` is the **parent** directory: `cd ..` climbs one level.
- `.` is the current directory itself.
- `cd -` jumps back to the previous directory, which is handy when you bounce between two places.

```
cd north/forest
pwd
cd ..
cd -
```

Real world: shells keep the previous directory in the variable `OLDPWD`, and `cd -` reads it. Two keystrokes save typing a long path twice.

objectives.text: Walk two levels deep in one command: cd north/forest
objectives.hint: From the lab root: cd north/forest

objectives.text: Climb up one level with cd ..
objectives.hint: .. always means the parent directory

objectives.text: Jump straight back to where you just were with cd -
objectives.hint: cd - toggles between your last two directories

lessons.title: Reading from afar
lessons.body:
You don't have to walk somewhere to read a file there. A path can point at it from anywhere:

- **Relative:** `../../south/river.txt` climbs two levels, then goes down into `south`.
- **Absolute:** `/lab/navigator/north/compass.txt` works from any directory.

`cat FILE` prints a file's contents.

```
cat ../../south/river.txt
cat /lab/navigator/north/compass.txt
```

Which one should you use? Relative paths are short and work wherever you copy the whole tree. Absolute paths are unambiguous, which is why scripts and config files prefer them.

objectives.text: From the forest, read the river note without moving: cat ../../south/river.txt
objectives.hint: From north/forest, two .. climb to the lab root; then go into south

objectives.text: Read the compass by its absolute path
objectives.hint: cat /lab/navigator/north/compass.txt

objectives.text: Go back to the lab root in a single cd
objectives.hint: Either cd ../.. or cd /lab/navigator works

lessons.title: The big picture
lessons.body:
Moving around with `cd` and `ls` is fine for a few directories. For a whole tree you want the overview:

- `tree DIR` draws the structure under `DIR`.
- `find DIR -name NAME` searches every directory under `DIR`, hidden ones included, and prints the path of each match.
- `find DIR -type d` lists only directories, and `-type f` lists only files.

```
tree /lab/navigator
find /lab/navigator -name gem.txt
```

Real world: `find / -name nginx.conf` is how you locate a config file on a machine you have never seen before. Pipe the result into other tools, and that comes in a later course.

objectives.text: Draw the whole lab as a tree: tree /lab/navigator
objectives.hint: tree DIR draws every directory under DIR

objectives.text: Hunt the gem by name: find /lab/navigator -name gem.txt
objectives.hint: find walks every directory, hidden ones too, and -name filters by file name

objectives.text: Read the gem's message
objectives.hint: Use the path find printed: cat /lab/navigator/south/.cave/gem.txt

courses.title: Reading the Runes
courses.summary: cat, head, tail, wc, nl and less: read any file without opening an editor.
courses.intro: Most of what a terminal shows you is text: logs, configs, notes, output. This course is about *reading* it well: all of it, the start, the end, or just how big it is. Your lab holds a ballad and a couple of notes.

files.ballad.txt:
There once was a shell in the deep,
Whose prompt never fell fast asleep.
It would cat and would grep,
Never missing a step,
And its pipes ran a hundred lines steep.

The novice would type and would stare,
At commands that went who-knows-where.
But with man at their side,
And a head held with pride,
They read every last line with care.

So read before running, my friend,
From the head of a file to its end.
files.notes/todo.txt:
read the ballad
count its lines
number the verses

lessons.title: Open the scroll
lessons.body:
Start in your lab: `cd /lab/reading`.

- `cat FILE` prints a file from top to bottom. The name comes from *concatenate*, because `cat` can join files together.
- `file PATH` tells you **what** something is before you open it: text, a directory, a program.

```
cat ballad.txt
file ballad.txt
file notes
```

Real world: run `file` on anything you downloaded before you `cat` it. Printing a binary file sprays garbage characters into your terminal.

objectives.text: Print the whole ballad with cat
objectives.hint: From /lab/reading: cat ballad.txt

objectives.text: Ask what kind of thing ballad.txt is with file
objectives.hint: file ballad.txt

objectives.text: Ask the same about notes
objectives.hint: file notes

lessons.title: Just the beginning, just the end
lessons.body:
Long files don't fit on one screen. You rarely need all of them anyway:

- `head FILE` shows the first 10 lines, and `head -n 3 FILE` shows the first 3.
- `tail FILE` shows the last 10, and `tail -n 2 FILE` shows the last 2.

```
head -n 3 ballad.txt
tail -n 2 ballad.txt
```

Real world: a log file grows at the bottom, so `tail` is where the news is. On a real system, `tail -f app.log` *follows* the file and prints new lines the moment they're written. That's how people watch a server live.

objectives.text: Show only the first 3 lines: head -n 3 ballad.txt
objectives.hint: head -n 3 ballad.txt

objectives.text: Show only the last 2 lines with tail
objectives.hint: tail -n 2 ballad.txt

lessons.title: How big is it?
lessons.body:
`wc` (*word count*) measures text:

- `wc -l` counts **lines**.
- `wc -w` counts **words**.
- `wc -c` counts **bytes**.
- a plain `wc` prints lines, words and bytes together.

```
wc -l ballad.txt
wc ballad.txt
```

Real world: "how many?" is the most common question you'll ask a terminal: how many errors, users, or files. `wc -l` is the usual answer, especially at the end of a pipeline, which is a later course.

objectives.text: Count the ballad's lines: wc -l ballad.txt
objectives.hint: -l counts lines

objectives.text: Count its words with wc -w
objectives.hint: -w counts words

objectives.text: Get lines, words and bytes at once with a plain wc
objectives.hint: wc with no flags prints all three counts

lessons.title: Numbered lines and paging
lessons.body:
- `nl FILE` prints a file with **line numbers**, which helps when someone says "look at line 7".
- `less FILE` is a **pager**. It shows one screen at a time: Space or PgDn goes forward, b or PgUp goes back, q quits. It never loads the whole file at once, so it opens huge logs instantly.

```
nl ballad.txt
less ballad.txt
```

Real world: `man` pages open in `less`. Anything you learn here (Space, b, q, and `/word` to search on a real system) works there too.

objectives.text: Number every line of the ballad with nl
objectives.hint: nl ballad.txt

objectives.text: Open the ballad in the pager: less ballad.txt (q quits)
objectives.hint: less ballad.txt, then Space for the next page, b to go back, q to quit

courses.title: The Pipeline Forge
courses.summary: grep, sort, uniq, cut and the | that joins them: answer real questions about real data.
courses.intro: The Unix idea fits in one sentence: **small tools, each doing one thing well, joined by pipes.** In this course you'll interrogate a guild's activity log and ledger, the same way you'd interrogate a web server's access log at work. Your lab holds `guild.log`, `ledger.csv` and `names.txt`.

files.guild.log:
2026-03-01 08:02 alice login
2026-03-01 08:05 alice deposit 40
2026-03-01 08:11 bob login
2026-03-01 08:13 bob withdraw 15
2026-03-01 08:30 cara login
2026-03-01 08:31 cara deposit 120
2026-03-01 09:00 alice logout
2026-03-01 09:12 dmitri login
2026-03-01 09:14 dmitri deposit 75
2026-03-01 09:40 bob deposit 10
2026-03-01 09:41 bob logout
2026-03-01 10:05 cara withdraw 30
2026-03-01 10:06 cara logout

2026-03-01 11:21 alice deposit 25

lessons.title: Searching with grep
lessons.body:
Start in your lab: `cd /lab/pipelines`.

`grep PATTERN FILE` prints every line of FILE that contains PATTERN. Its flags reshape the question:

- `-c`: *how many* lines match?
- `-v`: show the lines that *don't* match.
- `-i`: ignore case, so `alert` finds `ALERT`.
- `-n`: prefix each match with its line number.

```
grep alice guild.log
grep -c bob guild.log
grep -v login guild.log
```

Real world: `grep -i error /var/log/syslog` is step one of nearly every investigation. The pattern is a *regular expression*, so `grep '^2026-03-01 23'` finds everything from 23:00 on.

objectives.text: Find every line about alice: grep alice guild.log
objectives.hint: grep PATTERN FILE, from /lab/pipelines

objectives.text: Count bob's lines instead of printing them: grep -c bob guild.log
objectives.hint: -c prints only the number of matching lines

objectives.text: Show every line that is NOT a login: grep -v login guild.log
objectives.hint: -v inverts the match

objectives.text: Catch the alert whatever its case: grep -i alert guild.log
objectives.hint: -i ignores upper and lower case

lessons.title: Your first pipe
lessons.body:
The `|` (pipe) takes everything the command on its left **prints** and feeds it to the command on its right as **input**. Neither command knows the other exists.

```
cat guild.log | wc -l
grep deposit guild.log | wc -l
```

The second line asks *how many deposits were there?* `grep` answers "which lines?", `wc -l` answers "how many?", and the pipe composes them into a question neither tool can answer alone.

Real world: `ps aux | grep python | wc -l` counts how many Python processes are running. Same shape, different data.

objectives.text: Count the log's lines through a pipe: cat guild.log | wc -l
objectives.hint: The | sends cat's output into wc -l

objectives.text: Count only the deposits: grep deposit guild.log | wc -l
objectives.hint: grep picks the deposit lines; wc -l counts them

objectives.text: Keep just the first 5 lines of the log: cat guild.log | head -n 5
objectives.hint: head works on piped input too

lessons.title: Sorting and counting
lessons.body:
- `sort` puts lines in order: `-r` reverses it, and `-n` sorts by number instead of by text.
- `uniq` collapses **adjacent** duplicate lines, and `-c` counts them.

That word *adjacent* matters. `uniq` only compares each line with the one right before it, so you nearly always `sort` first:

```
uniq names.txt
sort names.txt | uniq
sort names.txt | uniq -c
```

Real world: `sort | uniq -c` is the shell's GROUP BY. It's how you count visitors per IP, errors per type, or commits per author.

objectives.text: Sort names.txt alphabetically
objectives.hint: sort names.txt

objectives.text: See why order matters: uniq names.txt (without sorting first)
objectives.hint: Run uniq straight on the file and compare with the sorted version

objectives.text: List each name once: sort names.txt | uniq
objectives.hint: Sort first, so duplicates sit next to each other

objectives.text: Count each name: sort names.txt | uniq -c
objectives.hint: -c prefixes each line with how many times it appeared

lessons.title: Columns with cut
lessons.body:
`ledger.csv` is **comma-separated values**: one record per line, with fields split by `,`. The first line is a header that names the fields: `date,member,action,gold`.

`cut` slices columns out of each line:

- `-d,` sets the field delimiter to a comma.
- `-f2` keeps the second field, `-f2,4` keeps fields two and four, and `-f2-` keeps everything from two on.

```
cut -d, -f2 ledger.csv
cut -d, -f2 ledger.csv | sort | uniq -c
```

Notice `member` in the count: the header row came along for the ride. `grep -v member` removes it.

Real world: exports from spreadsheets, databases and cloud consoles are almost always CSV. `cut` gives you answers in seconds, without opening a spreadsheet.

objectives.text: Pull out the member column: cut -d, -f2 ledger.csv
objectives.hint: -d, says fields are separated by commas; -f2 keeps field 2

objectives.text: Count rows per member: cut -d, -f2 ledger.csv | sort | uniq -c
objectives.hint: Three tools: cut picks the column, sort groups, uniq -c counts

objectives.text: Drop the header row with grep -v member ledger.csv
objectives.hint: The header is the only line containing the word member

lessons.title: Saving your work
lessons.body:
Output doesn't have to go to the screen:

- `cmd > FILE` writes the output into FILE, **replacing** whatever was there.
- `cmd >> FILE` **appends** to the end of FILE.

The redirect applies to the end of the whole pipeline:

```
grep alice guild.log > alice.txt
grep bob guild.log >> alice.txt
sort names.txt | uniq > roster.txt
cat roster.txt
```

Careful: `>` doesn't ask before it overwrites. `sort names.txt > names.txt` empties the file before `sort` even reads it. (Your lab is safe to break, and `lab reset` restores it.)

Real world: `command > output.txt 2>&1` saves both normal output and errors, which is how cron jobs keep their logs.

objectives.text: Save alice's lines to a file: grep alice guild.log > alice.txt
objectives.hint: > sends the output into a file instead of the screen

objectives.text: Append bob's lines to the same file: grep bob guild.log >> alice.txt
objectives.hint: >> adds to the end; a single > would replace alice's lines

objectives.text: Write a clean roster: sort names.txt | uniq > roster.txt
objectives.hint: Redirect the end of a whole pipeline

lessons.title: Capstone: the guild report
lessons.body:
Time to put the whole forge to work. The question: **which member made the most deposits?**

Build the answer one stage at a time. Run each line before adding the next stage:

```
grep deposit ledger.csv
grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2
grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c
grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn
grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1
```

`sort -rn` sorts by the count (`-n`, numerically) from biggest to smallest (`-r`), so `head -n 1` is the winner.

That six-stage pipeline is a real analytics query, written without a database. Swap `ledger.csv` for an access log and `-f2` for the IP column, and you've built "top 10 visitors" for a web server.

Tip: type `explain` right after running a pipeline, and each stage is broken down for you.

objectives.text: Find the member with the most deposits: grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1
objectives.hint: Build it one stage at a time and run it after each |
objectives.solution: grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn | head -n 1

objectives.text: Save the full ranking: grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > report.txt
objectives.hint: Same pipeline, minus head, plus > report.txt
objectives.solution: grep deposit ledger.csv | cut -d, -f2 | sort | uniq -c | sort -rn > report.txt

courses.title: The Artificer's Workshop
courses.summary: mkdir, touch, cp, mv, rm and chmod: create, organise and protect files.
courses.intro: Reading is half the job. The other half is changing things: making directories, moving files where they belong, deleting what you don't need, and marking scripts runnable. Your lab has an `inbox` that needs organising. It's a sandbox, so if something breaks, `lab reset` puts it back.

files.inbox/junk.tmp: temporary scratch data; safe to delete
files.inbox/notes.txt: Remember: copy before you change, and look before you delete.
files.inbox/report-draft.txt:
Quarterly report (draft)
- forge output up 12%
- two apprentices promoted

lessons.title: Making things
lessons.body:
Start in your lab: `cd /lab/workshop`.

- `mkdir NAME` makes a directory. On a real system, `mkdir -p a/b/c` makes the whole chain at once.
- `touch FILE` creates an empty file, or, if the file exists, updates its modification time and leaves the content alone.

```
mkdir archive
touch archive/index.txt
ls archive
```

Real world: `touch` is how you create a placeholder (`.gitkeep`) or a marker that a script checks for, like the `.statue_defeated` flag in this very game.

objectives.text: Build a new directory: mkdir archive
objectives.hint: From /lab/workshop: mkdir archive

objectives.text: Create an empty file inside it: touch archive/index.txt
objectives.hint: touch makes an empty file if none exists

objectives.text: Check your work: ls archive
objectives.hint: ls archive

lessons.title: Copying and moving
lessons.body:
- `cp SOURCE DEST` **copies**, so the original stays.
- `mv SOURCE DEST` **moves**, so the original is gone. There's no separate rename command: renaming is just moving to a new name.

If DEST is an existing directory, the file goes *inside* it and keeps its name.

```
cp inbox/notes.txt archive
mv inbox/report-draft.txt archive/report.txt
ls archive
```

Real world: before editing a config, copy it first. `cp nginx.conf nginx.conf.bak` is cheap insurance.

objectives.text: Copy inbox/notes.txt into archive: cp inbox/notes.txt archive
objectives.hint: When the destination is a directory, the copy keeps its name

objectives.text: Move and rename the draft in one step: mv inbox/report-draft.txt archive/report.txt
objectives.hint: mv SOURCE NEW-PATH both moves and renames

lessons.title: Removing things
lessons.body:
`rm FILE` deletes a file. **There is no trash can.** A shell `rm` is final.

That's why the habit is: **look, then delete.** Run `ls` (or `echo` the same glob) first, read what it would touch, and only then `rm`.

```
ls inbox
rm inbox/junk.tmp
ls inbox
```

Type `explain rm inbox/junk.tmp` before running it. `explain` flags dangerous commands.

Real world: `rm -rf` (recursive, force) on the wrong path is the classic career-ending typo. Many admins alias `rm` to `rm -i`, which asks before each deletion.

objectives.text: Delete the junk file: rm inbox/junk.tmp
objectives.hint: rm inbox/junk.tmp

objectives.text: Confirm it's gone: ls inbox
objectives.hint: ls inbox

lessons.title: Making it executable
lessons.body:
Every file carries **permissions**: who may **r**ead, **w**rite and e**x**ecute it. A script is only text until it has the execute permission:

- `chmod +x FILE` adds execute, and `chmod -x FILE` removes it.
- `ls -F` marks executables with `*`, and `ls -l` (on a real system) shows the full `rwxr-xr-x` string.

```
ls -F inbox
chmod +x inbox/spell.sh
ls -F inbox
```

Real world: "Permission denied" when you run `./deploy.sh` almost always means a missing `chmod +x`. The numeric form, `chmod 755 FILE`, sets all three permission groups at once.

objectives.text: Look at the scripts first: ls -F inbox
objectives.hint: ls -F marks executables with a *

objectives.text: Make the spell executable: chmod +x inbox/spell.sh
objectives.hint: +x adds the execute permission

objectives.text: Look again: ls -F inbox now shows spell.sh*
objectives.hint: The * after the name means executable

lessons.title: Writing files from the shell
lessons.body:
You don't need an editor for small files. `echo` plus a redirect is enough:

```
echo hello forge > note.txt
echo second line >> note.txt
cat note.txt
```

The rule from the pipelines course still holds: `>` replaces, `>>` appends.

Real world: `echo "export PATH=$HOME/bin:$PATH" >> ~/.bashrc` is how a lot of install instructions add a line to your shell config. Now you know why it's `>>`.

objectives.text: Write a note: echo hello forge > note.txt
objectives.hint: echo prints text; > sends it into a file

objectives.text: Add a second line: echo second line >> note.txt
objectives.hint: >> appends instead of replacing

objectives.text: Read it back: cat note.txt
objectives.hint: cat note.txt

courses.title: Words of Power
courses.summary: Variables, arithmetic, aliases, globs, quoting and history: make the shell work for you.
courses.intro: So far you've used the shell's commands. This course is about the shell *itself*: the features that make every command shorter, safer and repeatable. Your lab holds a few `spells/` and a grimoire.

files.grimoire.md:
# The Grimoire of Words of Power

Variables remember. Aliases shorten. Globs multiply. Quotes protect. History never forgets.
files.spells/fire.txt: Ignis: a spell of warmth and light.
files.spells/ice.txt: Glacies: a spell that slows the world down.

lessons.title: Variables
lessons.body:
A **variable** is a name for a value. `export NAME=value` creates one, and `$NAME` uses it anywhere in a command line.

```
export GUILD=forge
echo $GUILD
env
```

Two rules trip everyone up once:

- There are **no spaces around `=`**. `export GUILD = forge` is three separate words.
- Names are case-sensitive, so `$GUILD` and `$guild` are different variables.

Real world: `$HOME`, `$PATH` and `$USER` are variables your system set for you. Programs read `$PATH` to decide where commands live.

objectives.text: Create a variable: export GUILD=forge
objectives.hint: No spaces around the =: export GUILD=forge

objectives.text: Read it back: echo $GUILD
objectives.hint: The $ asks the shell for the variable's value

objectives.text: See every variable at once with env
objectives.hint: env prints NAME=value for every exported variable

lessons.title: Arithmetic
lessons.body:
Shell variables hold **text**. To do arithmetic, you have to ask for it:

```
export MANA=10
let MANA=MANA+5
echo $MANA
```

Inside `let`, names are read as numbers, so no `$` is needed. Bash also has `$(( MANA + 5 ))`, which you'll meet in real scripts.

This game uses the same trick: your health lives in `$HP`, and `let HP=HP-5` is how a monster hurts you.

objectives.text: Store a number: export MANA=10
objectives.hint: export MANA=10

objectives.text: Add to it with let: let MANA=MANA+5
objectives.hint: Inside let you write MANA without the $

objectives.text: Check the result: echo $MANA
objectives.hint: echo $MANA

lessons.title: Aliases
lessons.body:
An **alias** is a nickname for a longer command line. The shell swaps it in before running anything.

```
alias ll='ls -F'
ll
alias
```

The quotes matter: without them, `alias ll=ls -F` gives the alias only `ls`, and `-F` becomes a separate argument.

Real world: aliases live in `~/.bashrc` or `~/.zshrc`, so they load in every new shell. Common ones are `ll`, `la`, `..='cd ..'`, and `gs='git status'`.

objectives.text: Make a shortcut: alias ll='ls -F'
objectives.hint: Quote the command so the space stays inside it

objectives.text: Use it: type ll
objectives.hint: Just ll, and the shell expands it to ls -F

objectives.text: List your aliases: alias
objectives.hint: alias with no arguments lists them all

lessons.title: Globs and quotes
lessons.body:
Start in your lab: `cd /lab/shell-craft`.

A **glob** is a filename pattern: `*` matches any run of characters, and `?` matches exactly one character. The **shell** expands a glob into matching names *before* the command runs. `echo` never sees the `*`.

```
echo spells/*.txt
echo 'spells/*.txt'
find . -name '*.log'
```

**Quotes** stop the expansion. That's why `find -name '*.log'` is quoted: you want `find` to receive the pattern and match it in every directory, not have the shell replace it with whatever matches *here*.

Type `explain echo spells/*.txt` to see what the glob expands to.

objectives.text: Let the shell expand a glob: echo spells/*.txt
objectives.hint: * matches any run of characters within one name

objectives.text: Quote it and the shell leaves it alone: echo 'spells/*.txt'
objectives.hint: Single quotes stop expansion

objectives.text: Hand the pattern to find instead: find . -name '*.log'
objectives.hint: Quoted, so find (not the shell) does the matching, in every subdirectory

lessons.title: History never forgets
lessons.body:
Every line you type is remembered. `history` lists them, and the Up and Down arrows walk back through them.

```
history
history > history.txt
```

On a real bash shell you also get:

- `!!`: run the last command again (`sudo !!` is a classic).
- `Ctrl+R`: search your history as you type.
- `~/.bash_history`: where it all persists between sessions.

That's the whole course: variables remember, aliases shorten, globs multiply, quotes protect, and history never forgets. You now have the vocabulary to read almost any shell script you come across.

objectives.text: Review what you've typed: history
objectives.hint: history lists your recent command lines

objectives.text: Keep a record: history > history.txt
objectives.hint: Redirect history into a file like any other output
